content.title: Response to reviewer RHGU
content.comment:
>“They do not show why expensive model-based approaches are not practical or how much the proposed model shortened learning/inference time.”

Our method does not introduce additional hyper-parameters. This means that the hyper-parameter search space associated with our method is smaller. Thus, unlike model-based methods that introduce hyper-parameters (eg BC + BB), our method trains much faster. For example, state of the art model-based method BC+BB requires tuning a scalar for an additional loss function as well as choosing the right set of augmentation functions; both parameters change across datasets. Therefore, by introducing a hyper-parameter-free approach, our method trains faster and is more likely to generalize. We will revise our paper to clarify this point.


>“In section 4.3, there is no detail of how the percentage value x is applied to the proposed model.”

We thank the reviewer for pointing out this potential point of confusion. We agree that this could be further clarified. Given two classes $c_1$ and $c_2$ where we seek to subsample $c_2$ in order to mimic $c_1$ bias, we could alternatively mimic a percentage of $c_1$ bias. Assume $c_1$ bias toward bias group $b_1$ is $P(B=b_1 | Y=c_1)$, then we could mimic instead half of that, i.e,  $P(B=b_1 | Y=c_1)/2$. The percentage then refers to the chosen value of mimicking that could range between $P(B=b_1 | Y=c_1)$ (%100) and $P(B=b_1 | Y=c_2)$ (%0). We will revise the paper with these details. 


>“In table 3, there is no detail of exactly what class 1 and class 2 are”

In this table, we carry out the experiment on the binary classification tasks from the datasets: UTK-Face and CelebA. Therefore, for each task, we are predicting two classes. Class 1 and Class 2 therefore refer to these classes.

>“The evaluation metrics and competitors of the binary classification benchmark and the multi-class classification benchmark are different. And there is a lack of explanation as to why they should be different.”

We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. The two benchmarks are borrowed from two different papers. To stay consistent with prior work, we kept their metrics. However, we agree unifying the metrics might bring additionality clarity to the relative difficulties of the tasks.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Data resampling and upweighting are widely adopted in bias mitigation task, but it suffers from training stability or model capacity. To handle this issue, the authors propose bias mimicking for class-conditioned sampling method. They first create a different version of class target labels, where the bias of y is mimicked (under-sampled) that of other classes. When mimicking, they train a binary classifier to predict y (y or not y), and this mimicking is conducted for all classes, which prevents dropping a large amount of data for undersampling. The proposed framework is evaluated on binary-class and multi-class benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strength
- They propose a bias mimicking that conduct undersampling in an efficient way that minimizes sample drop.
- The results show competitive performance compared to existing approaches.

### Weakness
- Average accuracy is missing. I encourage the authors to include the average accuracy for all tables (in addition to UA and BC) for all methods for a comprehensive view.
- In cost analysis, why (Wang et al.) is O(B) and BM is O(1)? In my understanding, (Wang et al.) employs multi-way classifiers, but the cost of forwarding classification layer is negligible compared to feature extractor, so the overall cost will almost be the same. In a similar vein, I don’t think ‘additional model params’ in main tables is useful. Also, what does the ‘additional hyperparameters’ mean for each method?
- During training, the proposed method requires two-stage training, 1) bias mimicking and 2) upsampling, but such limitation is not addressed.
- In Ch4.3, comparing with OS/UW/US will provide more accurate analysis. Could you provide the results by changing the percentage value of sampling or weighting of OS/UW/WS, as in Ch 4.3?
- Experimental results are not strong, especially compared to the sampling strategies.
- Ablative study is incomplete.
    - 1) How is the results when feature extractor is trained with multiple binary classifier without bias mimicking, and then OS/UW/WS? (In other words, only bias mimicking is removed in the full framework.)
    - 2) What will be the results if stop gradient is not used to train final model?

content.title: Response to reviewer 6vhq
content.comment:
>Average accuracy is missing.

The average accuracy in this problem setup is a misleading metric. This is because the test set is biased toward some subgroups more than others. Therefore, the metric does not reflect how the model performs on *all* subgroups. A vanilla (biased) model, for example, might have a higher average accuracy than an unbiased model if the test set was heavily skewed toward one subgroup. Thus,  unbiased accuracy is often used in the fairness literature (Hong & Yang (2021)  as a more robust version of averaged accuracy. This is because it takes the mean of accuracy on each subgroup separately.


>In cost analysis, why (Wang et al.) is O(B) and BM is O(1)? In my understanding, (Wang et al.) employs multi-way classifiers, but the cost of forwarding classification layer is negligible compared to feature extractor, so the overall cost will almost be the same.

Wang et al. introduces a multi-class prediction head for each subgroup (intersection of class and bias membership). The number of subgroups equals the number of bias groups multiplied by the number of classes. For example, 10 classes and 10 bias groups results in 99 extra prediction head. This increase will have an impact on inference time and is not necessarily scalable as we further increase the number of bias groups and classes. 

>What does the ‘additional hyperparameters’ mean for each method?

Methods labeled with additional hyper-parameters mean that they introduce additional loss functions that require hyper-parameter tuning. For example, BC+BB  (Hong & Yang (2021)  requires a scalar parameter to optimize an additional loss. It also requires choosing augmentation function for its contrastive learning paradigms which needs to be tuned according to the dataset. Our method does not. Therefore, the hyper-parameter search space associated with our method is smaller.

>Experimental results are not strong, especially compared to the sampling strategies.

We note that while our method only improves slightly over upweighting on the Binary Classification Benchmark, it improves by a big margin on the multi-class classification benchmark. More concrelty, it improves by >%7. Therefore, our method is the only sampling method with consistently stable performance. Compared to nonsampling methods, our method improves averaged accuracies over state of the art on the binary classification benchmark by 3%. On the multi classification benchmark, while our method obtains the same performance as Domain Independence, Domain Independance performs considerably worse than our method on the binary classification benchmark.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a resampling-based approach to reduce bias of classifier predictions towards a sensitive attribute. The method, termed bias mimicking, first converts a K-way classification into K binary problems, and undersamples the data for each problem to achieve statistical independence between target label and bias attribute. A multi-way classification head is then trained on top of the frozen feature extractor to make the final prediction. Bias mimicking achieves state-of-the-art results on binary and mult-class datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Pros
- The overall idea of removing statistical dependency between target and bias attributes makes intuitive sense. I agree with authors that data imbalance is the main source of model bias, and that more effort should be devoted towards fixing the bias in the training data.
- Unlike most prior works on debiasing that focused on binary classification, this work can be applied to multi-class problems.  
- The proposed method produces similar results to strong debiasing baselines, while not requiring additional modules or hyperparameter tuning. Main results are provided with mean/std over multiple runs. 

## Cons
- I feel that the presentation of bias mimicking (sec 3.2) needs more work. The current version lacks clarity, making the key idea of the work quite hard to comprehend.  
	- $d_y$ is defined as “a different version of target label” for class $y$ , without further explanation on its value range, or how it is obtained from $y$ .  
	- It is unclear what $P_{d_y}$ means in equation 1, or how the resampling should be performed to ensure the statistical independence.  
	- Can the authors elaborate on how the method differs from naive undersampling on binary classification datasets?  
	- While figure 2 helps understanding the method in an abstract level, it would be ideal to include an algorithm that details each step of the training procedure. 
- On experiments:  
	- On binary attributes it would be ideal if more attributes on CelebA are included (e.g. following [BPA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.02943)). While some attributes like "heavy makeup" is subjective and noisy (as identified in this work), others such as "wearing lipstick", "double chin" might be good options.  
	- The paper is missing some important work on bias mitigation such as [Group DRO](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.08731), which optimizes a worst-group training loss combined with group-balanced resampling.  
	- I wonder if the additional binary classification heads count as additional model parameters in table 1 and 2, or are the extra parameters negligible compared to baseline models? 
- Minor errors / typos
	- In page 5, I did not understand the argument "Consequently, since each $d_y$ preserves $y$ samples...". Can the authors clarify its meaning?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As discussed above, I am concerned about the clarity of the writing. Without fully understanding the mechanisms of the proposed bias mimicking approach, it is difficult to evaluate the importance of its contribution relative to prior methods based on resampling. On the brighter side, training code is provided which adds to the reproducibility of the work.
content.summary_of_the_review: While this paper brings some interesting insights to the effectiveness of data resampling for bias mitigation, I feel that it is not yet ready for publication due to the lack of clarity in its writing, and some missing experimental results/comparisons. I look forward to the responses and clarifications from the authors in the discussion period.

content.title: Response to reviewer wdPT
content.comment:
>“d_y is defined as “a different version of target label” for class , without further explanation on its value range, or how it is obtained from y.”

>“It is unclear what P_{d_y} means in equation 1, or how the resampling should be performed to ensure the statistical independence.“

>“Can the authors elaborate on how the method differs from naive undersampling on binary classification datasets?”

Thank you for your suggestions on how to improve the clarity of the approach in our paper. We offer a revised notation below and hope that it clarifies our approach. 

Assume $Y$ is the set of target labels, $B$ is the set of bias labels, $C$ is the set of classes, and $S$ is the set of bias groups, then: 

The key principle of our algorithm is the observation that if the distribution of bias groups with respect to a class $c$ (\ie $P_D(B | Y = c)$), was the same across every $c \in C$, then $B$ is statistically independent from $Y$. 

We use this result to motivate a novel way of subsampling the input distribution that ensures the model is exposed to every sample in the dataset. To that end, for every class $c \in C$, we produce a subsampled version of the Dataset $D$ denoted as $d_c \subset D$. Each $d_c$ preserves its respective class $c$ samples (\ie $d_c$ contains all of $c$ samples) while subsampling every $c^{\prime} \neq c$ such that the bias distribution of bias groups in class $c$ is mimicked in each $c^{\prime}$. Formally:

$P_{d_c}(B=s | Y = c) = P_{d_c}(B = s | Y = c^{\prime}) \quad \forall s \in S$

Note since $Y$ is statistically independent of $B$ in each $d_c$, then the model is unlikely to spuriously correlate $Y$ with $B$. Furthermore, since each $d_c$ does not subsample $c$ samples (\ie $d_c$ contains all of $c$ samples), by using every $d_c$ to train the model, the model is then exposed to the entire dataset. This is unlike Undersampling where every subgroup, and as a proxy class, needs to be subsampled. 

> I wonder if the additional binary classification heads count as additional model parameters in table 1 and 2, or are the extra parameters negligible compared to baseline models?

Note that each binary prediction head is simply one output node trained with Binary Cross entropy. Therefore, when considered together, the binary prediction heads introduce no extra model parameters compared to a multi class prediction head. Our only additional cost is the multi-class prediction that we use to perform inference. However, since it is only one linear layer that does not update the feature encoder, its cost is negligible.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focused on the task of bias mitigation in visual recognition datasets, where there exist strong spurious correlations between class and a dataset-sensitive group. Previous works mainly focused on model-based solutions, which require additional parameters during inference or expensive hyper-parameter tuning for additional losses during training. To overcome these limitations, this work extended data re-sampling methods to bias mitigation tasks, and proposed a class-conditioned sampling method called Bias Mimicking (BM). BM creates a different version of dataset target labels where the bias within other classes mimics that of the target class. Besides, this paper provided an extensive analysis on sampling methods for bias mitigation tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

\+ Novel motivation. This paper focused on the task of bias mitigation in visual recognition datasets. While previous works mainly focused on model modification or loss design, this work proposed to extend data re-sampling strategies, which is more efficient and free of hyperparameters. The motivation is novel to me

\+ Simple but efffective method. The method is consistent with the motivation.  The idea is straightforward and makes sense.

\+ Analysis of re-sampling methods in bias mitigation. This paper further provide an analysis of re-sampling methods in bias mitigation, which is lacking in previous studies. This analysis helps to understand the role of re-sampling methods and may inspire future research in this direction.

\+ Satisfying writing quality. The paper is well-organized and written. It is easy and straightforward to understand the core ideas and contributions.


Weaknesses & Questions

\- The role of feature encoder in bias mimicking. In Figure 2, the feature encoder is used for bias mimicking. It is not to me the role of feature encoder in bias mimicking. Based on my understanding, the bias mimicking is based on known bias rather than features. How are features used to mimick the bias?

\- Extension of re-weighting. This work focused on how to adapt re-sampling to bias mitigation tasks, and also compared their method with both re-sampling and re-weighting baselines. I am wondering whether the bias mimicking idea can be used on re-weighting methods, as one can create a similar version by assigning samples with different weights. If not, what is the reason? Such discussion would make the paper more self-contained and complete.

\- Whether bias is known. There are two settings for bias mitigation according to whether the bias of the dataset is known or available. According to the description of the method, it seems that this method can only work when the bias is known, which might be a limitation of this method. If so, it would be great to include the detailed discussion of limitations. Please correct my if I misunderstood the idea.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The quality, clarity and originality of the work is good. Please see Strenths for detailed comments.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, I am leaning positive.

This paper focused on the task of bias mitigation in visual recognition datasets. The strengths of this paper are that (1) the bias mitigation problem is fundemental and important in AI fairness, (2) the motivation of this paper is reasonable, (3) the proposed idea is consistent with the motivation, (4) an empirical analysis of re-sampling methods in bias mitigation is conducted, and (5) its writing quality. 

The weaknesses and concerns are that (1) the role of feature encoder in bias mimicking is not clear to me, (2) the discussion of extending re-weighting methods to bias mimicking is lacking or not clear, (3) the discussion of experimental settings about bias is not clear.

Considering both strengths and weaknesses, I vote for acceptance based on the overall quality of this paper.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.

content.title: Response to reviewer 91iN
content.comment:
>“The role of feature encoder in bias mimicking. In Figure 2, the feature encoder is used for bias mimicking. It is not to me the role of feature encoder in bias mimicking. Based on my understanding, the bias mimicking is based on known bias rather than features. How are features used to mimic the bias?”

The feature encoder is a standard part of Deep Learning Computer Vision models. It takes the input images and produces a feature embedding which is then fed to a linear predictive layer for inference. The feature encoder is not used differently with bias mimicking than other methods. The resulting feature embeddings are used to train the prediction heads outlined in Figure 2 in an end to end fashion. Since we train two different prediction heads for Bias Mimicking (one of which is discarded at test time), we differentiate between the feature encoder and the heads in Figure 2 purely for clarification purposes.


>“Extension of re-weighting. This work focused on how to adapt re-sampling to bias mitigation tasks, and also compared their method with both re-sampling and re-weighting baselines. I am wondering whether the bias mimicking idea can be used on re-weighting methods, as one can create a similar version by assigning samples with different weights. If not, what is the reason? Such discussion would make the paper more self-contained and complete.”

We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion. Indeed, bias mimicking can be used with upweighting. Standard upweighting equalizes the contribution of each sample by multiplying its loss value by 1/(probability of sampling the sample's subgroup). However, in the spirit of Bias Mimicking, we can derive the weights using the Bias Mimicking assumption. 

>“Whether bias is known. There are two settings for bias mitigation according to whether the dataset's bias is known or available. According to the description of the method, it seems that this method can only work when the bias is known, which might be a limitation of this method. If so, it would be great to include the detailed discussion of limitations. Please correct my if I misunderstood the idea.”

In this paper we explored a setting where we assume some labels for sensitive attributes are available. While there is some prior work that attempts to mitigate bias when these attributes are not available, the final performance does not match methods where the bias labels are known. Nevertheless, we agree it is important to highlight these differences. Therefore, we will add this discussion to our limitations.
